profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at Meridian Industrial Holdings to prepare a September pension committee workshop for its frozen defined benefit plan, which is currently near full funding and could move into either underfunded or overfunded territory over the next few years depending on rates, markets, and contribution policy. The company wants to present a practical asset-liability strategy using cash, long-duration bonds, and equities, along with a funding policy that adapts when the plan moves above or below target. The agenda is to decide what analysis package will be built for the board, what assumptions will be used in the scenario work, who owns each workstream, and the timeline for drafting the board materials. The expected outcome is a shared workplan for producing a board deck, scenario outputs, and an implementation timetable for a proposed funding-and-investment policy review.

members.name: Elena Park
members.expertise: Defined benefit funding policy, actuarial valuations, sponsor contribution planning
members.background: Elena is a credentialed actuary who moved from a consulting firm into corporate benefits and now manages long-range pension strategy, including funded-status projections and board materials for the pension committee.
members.private_state: She wants the board workshop to endorse a policy framework that makes the sponsor's future contribution obligations look stable and disciplined, while avoiding a debate that reopens last year's valuation assumptions.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the plan's 'current spread schedule,' they mean the closed amortization layers already embedded in the formal funding policy approved at the January valuation.

References to 'the stress scenario we showed the board last year' point to the actuarial downside case used in the pension committee workshop, not the treasury team's market-risk appendix from a different meeting.
A probability of being underfunded or overfunded should be measured on funded status after scheduled sponsor contributions are applied, because that is the status the board governs.
A deliverable is 'board-ready' once it reconciles to the actuarial liability basis and contribution schedule, even if market values are a few days behind the custodian file.

members.name: Daniel Reed
members.expertise: Portfolio construction, liability-aware investing, market risk reporting
members.background: Daniel came from an asset-management background and now oversees the company's pension asset managers, hedge positioning, and investment reporting to finance and the pension committee.
members.private_state: He wants the workshop to create room for a more responsive de-risking framework tied to market conditions, without committing the investment team to a rigid contribution-driven policy that reduces portfolio discretion.
hidden_assumptions: The 'current spread schedule' is the rolling 12-year amortization approach finance uses for planning cash contributions in annual budgeting, not the closed layers from the actuarial policy memo.

When someone mentions 'the board stress scenario from last year,' they are referring to the treasury shock set included in the November board appendix because that is the one directors actually questioned him about.
The probability of ending underfunded or overfunded should isolate investment performance against liabilities before sponsor catch-up contributions, otherwise the investment policy signal is blurred.
A deliverable is 'board-ready' if the asset numbers tie to the latest custodian positions and the directional conclusions are stable, even if actuarial reconciliation is finished afterward.

misalignment_points.topic: Meaning of the current spread schedule
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to run the strategy under 'the current 12-year spread schedule.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the closed amortization layers in the formal funding policy, where each deficit base is amortized over a fixed 12-year period from the valuation date.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means an open, rolling 12-year amortization schedule that gets refreshed each year for budgeting purposes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are accustomed to calling their own version simply 'the current spread schedule,' and because they are not debating the contribution policy itself, the phrase sounds settled rather than in need of unpacking.

misalignment_points.topic: Which prior board stress case to reuse
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to anchor the materials on 'the stress scenario we showed the board last year.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the pension committee workshop scenario with a 100 basis point rate decline, 18% equity drop, and revised liability discounting used in the actuarial valuation discussion.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the treasury appendix scenario with a 75 basis point rate decline, 12% equity drop, and credit-spread widening used in the November board finance pack.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both meetings involved the same directors, both happened 'last year,' and each participant interacted most closely with a different deck, so the shorthand reference feels mutually obvious.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the probability of being underfunded
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to show 'the probability of ending underfunded versus overfunded at the horizon.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 will classify outcomes using terminal funded ratio after scheduled contributions under the spread method have been paid and benefits/obligations are rolled forward on the actuarial basis.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 will classify outcomes using market asset value relative to projected liabilities before sponsor remedial contributions, so the statistic reflects portfolio risk rather than sponsor support.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like a straightforward output rather than a constructed measure, and each discipline treats its own convention as the natural one for pension reporting.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that Daniel will provide 'board-ready numbers' for the first draft by the end of the month.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects numbers that already reconcile to the actuarial liability projection set and can be dropped directly into the committee deck with only formatting edits.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects to deliver indicative portfolio results tied to the custodian file and manager exposures, with actuarial reconciliation to follow in the next iteration.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In competent corporate settings, 'board-ready' often refers to polish and usefulness rather than a formal gate, so each person hears the phrase as confirming normal standards without realizing their completion criteria differ.

turns.inner_thought: This workshop needs to come across as one coherent framework, not a loose discussion that invites the committee to reopen last year's valuation assumptions. If I keep the conversation centered on an integrated funding-and-investment path, I can steer them toward a disciplined policy story and stable sponsor contributions.
turns.utterance: I think the September committee session should be framed as one integrated approach, not separate funding and asset conversations. We need to show how the plan behaves if it moves below target and if it moves above target over the next few years, and what the company would actually do in each case.

turns.inner_thought: That works for me as long as the investment piece stays practical and gives us room to talk about responsive de-risking. If the board sees how the cash, long bond, and equity mix behaves under different funded-status paths, I can create space for a framework tied to market conditions rather than a rigid contribution-led policy.
turns.utterance: Yes, agreed. If we do it well, the materials can show how the cash, bond, and equity mix behaves across those funded-status paths so the board sees the implementation side, not just the policy language.

turns.inner_thought: For the baseline, we should use the formal funding policy already approved in January: the closed amortization layers embedded in the valuation work. Everyone refers to that as the current spread schedule anyway, and it avoids any need to revisit the assumption set.
turns.utterance: For the baseline runs, I'd like to keep the contribution side on the current 12-year spread schedule so we're comparing strategies against a consistent policy path.

turns.inner_thought: Using the current spread schedule is fine; finance already plans around the rolling 12-year amortization approach in the budget, so that should make the contribution path familiar and keep this from turning into a separate funding-policy fight. Good to have that settled quickly.

turns.inner_thought: For the downside anchor, we should simply reuse the actuarial stress case from the pension committee workshop last year. The directors already saw that framework in the valuation discussion, so it keeps continuity and avoids introducing a fresh debate.
turns.utterance: On the downside framing, I'd prefer to anchor the materials on the stress scenario we showed the board last year. That way the directors don't have to learn a brand-new setup before they react to the strategy.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. I'll refresh the treasury shock set from the November appendix since that's the one the directors actually pushed on, and I can update it cleanly with current market levels and manager exposures. turns.utterance: Yes, I can refresh that same board stress scenario with current market levels and manager exposures so the comparison still feels intuitive.

turns.inner_thought: The committee will want a simple summary metric, and for governance purposes it needs to be funded status at horizon after scheduled sponsor contributions under the spread method. That's the relevant decision lens for the board: whether the plan ends up underfunded or overfunded once the policy contributions have been made.
turns.utterance: I'd also like the deck to show the probability of ending underfunded versus overfunded at the horizon. The committee is going to want to see how often the strategy lands on either side over the planning window.

turns.inner_thought: That's a useful board metric if I define it the usual investment way—market asset value against projected liabilities before sponsor catch-up contributions. That will preserve the portfolio signal and let me pair it with a clean risk-return chart in the appendix.
turns.utterance: I can produce those underfunded and overfunded probabilities from the scenario engine and pair them with an efficient-frontier style chart for the appendix so they have both the headline view and the trade-off view.

turns.inner_thought: I need his outputs early enough to drop directly into the committee deck, and to be useful they have to reconcile to the actuarial liability basis and contribution schedule. If I say board-ready numbers, that should be clear enough; then I can build the narrative without scrambling at the end.

turns.inner_thought: End of month is manageable if board-ready means a polished draft tied to the latest custodian file and current exposures, with the actuarial tie-out finishing afterward. I'll send Elena an indicative pack first so we can shape the story before the final version hardens.
turns.utterance: Yes, that's workable. I'll get you board-ready numbers by month-end, and before that I'll send a draft pack so we can align the story before final formatting.
